mainTopic: Weakened documents, a borrower's promise to trust the lender, and oaths involving a minor or an heir
overview: This amud covers several cases about debts, documents and oaths. First it finishes the gallnuts story: witnesses prove the borrower named a false market price, and רבא rules he is a כפרן, because people do remember the set market price. Next, a lender with a שטר admits he was paid but says the money was for other debts. רב נחמן says the שטר is weakened, and רב פפא says it is not. The final הלכה is that the שטר is weakened, but only when the payment was made in front of witnesses. In a private payment the lender is believed because of a מיגו. Then the גמרא discusses a borrower who promised to believe the lender about non-payment. It asks whether that promise beats witnesses, and whether 'like two witnesses' covers three. Here רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע teaches that in testimony two are like a hundred, unlike counting opinions. Finally, the גמרא explains why no oath is taken on a minor's claim. It shows that the משנה's 'we swear to a קטן' means an adult heir claiming his father's debt, following רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

steps.title: The gallnuts price is proven wrong by witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The borrower claims he paid with gallnuts worth six per measure. The lender says they were worth four, and two witnesses back up the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: The borrower said: 'Didn't I pay you with gallnuts that were selling at six dinars each measure?' The lender said: 'Weren't they selling at only four?' Two witnesses came and said: 'Yes, they were selling at four.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a story that began before this section: a borrower says he paid his debt with gallnuts, and they now argue about how much those gallnuts were worth. Witnesses come and support the lender's price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower valued his payment at six per measure, which would cover more of the debt. The witnesses prove the real price was four, so the borrower's account of his payment is shown to be false. This sets up רבא's ruling in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Gallnuts, a valuable product used for making ink and dye
Literally 'standing'; here it means 'were selling at' a certain price

phrases.english: ...gallnuts that were selling at six, six [dinars per measure]?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״לָאו בְּאַרְבְּעָה אַרְבָּעָה הֲווֹ קָיְימִי?״
phrases.english: He said to him: Weren't they selling at four, four?
Two witnesses came and said:
Yes, they were selling at four, four.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a case story that began before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The facts are established: the gallnuts were worth four, not six, as the borrower claimed.

steps.title: רבא: The borrower is now considered a denier
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that since witnesses proved the borrower wrong, he now has the status of a כפרן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: He is now established as a denier.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his ruling on the gallnuts case. Because the witnesses proved the borrower's claim false, he is treated as someone who denies his debts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower tried to count his payment as worth more than it really was. Once witnesses contradicted him, רבא treats him as a person who falsely denied part of his debt. That status affects how much he is trusted from now on.

keyTerms.meaning: He is established as / given the status of
A denier: someone who falsely denies owing money

phrases.english: Rava said: He is established as a denier.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the facts set out in step 1
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A borrower whose payment claim is disproven by witnesses gets the status of a כפרן.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא: Maybe he simply forgot
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא challenges רבא using רבא's own principle: people don't keep in mind things they have no reason to remember.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: But you yourself said that anything a person has no responsibility for, he doesn't keep in his mind!
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא challenges רבא's ruling. He quotes a rule רבא taught earlier and argues that the borrower may have just forgotten the price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא taught that people don't pay attention to details they have no duty to track. If so, the borrower could have honestly mixed up the gallnuts price, and that is not lying. Then why call him a כפרן?

keyTerms.meaning: Not placed upon him, meaning something he has no responsibility for
Not on his mind; he doesn't pay attention to it

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama said:
But you said: any matter
phrases.notes: He is quoting a rule רבא himself taught earlier.

phrases.english: that is not placed upon a person
is not on his mind!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא אָמְרַתְּ כֹּל מִילְּתָא דְּלָא רַמְיָא עֲלֵיהּ דְּאִינִישׁ לָאו אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's ruling in step 2
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the borrower is a כפרן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By רבא's own principle, a person may honestly forget details he isn't responsible for. So a wrong price may be an innocent mistake, not a lie.

steps.title: רבא: Everyone remembers the market price
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the fixed market price is something people do remember.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: The fixed market price is something people definitely remember.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge. His forgetting rule doesn't apply here, because a known market price is not the kind of detail people forget.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא doesn't take back his rule. He limits it: small personal details may be forgotten, but the public price everyone knows is remembered. So the borrower's wrong price was not an honest slip, and he stays a כפרן.

keyTerms.meaning: The fixed price of the market
They certainly remember (the doubled verb adds emphasis)

steps.whatToRemember: A person who claims a false market price is treated as a כפרן. He cannot say he forgot, because people remember the set market price.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
The fixed market price, people certainly remember.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the principle
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower might have just forgotten the price, like any detail he isn't responsible for.
steps.terutzMaskana: A set market price is common knowledge that people remember, so getting it wrong counts as denial.

steps.title: New case: 'I paid you' — 'That was a different loan'
steps.stepSummary: A lender demands 100 dinars and shows a שטר. The borrower says he already paid, and the lender says that money was for other loans.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said to another: 'Give me the 100 dinars you owe me, and here is the שטר.' The other said: 'I already paid you.' The lender said: 'That money was for other debts.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story. This step lays out the facts, and the next step brings the rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender admits he received money but says it covered a different debt. The question is whether that admission weakens the שטר he is holding now.

keyTerms.meaning: That I claim from you / that you owe me
A promissory note: a written document proving a loan
Other / different matters, meaning other debts

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to his fellow:
Give me a hundred dinars
that I claim from you, and here is the document.
He said to him: I repaid you.
He said to him: Those were other [debts].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case, unrelated to the gallnuts story
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets out the case: the lender admits he was paid but claims it was for different debts.

steps.title: רב נחמן and רב פפא argue about the note
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says the שטר is weakened. רב פפא says it is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The שטר is weakened. רב פפא said: The שטר is not weakened.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים disagree about the case in step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן holds that once the lender admits he received a payment, his claim that it was for a different loan has no proof, so the שטר loses its strength. רב פפא holds that the claim of other loans is believable, so the שטר keeps its force.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: The document is weakened.

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: לָא אִיתְּרַע שְׁטָרָא.
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: The document is not weakened.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives two opposing rulings on the case in step 5
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן: the שטר is weakened. רב פפא: the שטר stays valid.

steps.title: רב פפא's own oxen ruling seems to contradict him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points to another case where רב פפא ruled the שטר is weakened: the borrower said the money was for oxen and the lender was paid from the oxen.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רב פפא, how is this different from a case where a man said: 'Give me the 100 dinars you owe me, here is the שטר,' and the other answered: 'Didn't you give me the money for oxen, and then you came, sat at the slaughterhouse, and got your money back?' The lender said: 'That was for other debts.' And there רב פפא said: the שטר is weakened.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא with a ruling of his own. In a very similar case he said the שטר is weakened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cases look the same: the lender admits he got paid and claims it was for a different loan. In the oxen case רב פפא said the שטר is weakened, yet here he says it is not. That looks like a contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? (a question pointing out an apparent contradiction)

steps.confusionAlert: Both opinions here belong to רב פפא. The question is not רב נחמן against רב פפא; it is רב פפא against himself.

phrases.english: And according to Rav Pappa, what is different
from that one who said to his fellow:
Give me a hundred dinars
that I claim from you, and here is the document;
He said to him: Didn't you give it to me for oxen,
phrases.notes: The money was given to buy oxen for slaughter, and the lender was to be paid back from selling the meat.

phrases.english: and you came and sat at the slaughterhouse
and received your money?
And he said to him: Those were other [debts];
And Rav Pappa said: The document is weakened.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's opinion from step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that the שטר is not weakened
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the oxen case, which looks just like this one, רב פפא ruled the שטר is weakened. His two rulings seem to contradict each other.

steps.title: The oxen case named a specific deal
steps.stepSummary: In the oxen case the borrower described one specific deal and its payback, so 'other debts' is not believable. In the plain 'I paid you' case, other debts is a reasonable possibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, since the borrower said: 'You gave me money for oxen, and you were paid from the oxen,' the שטר is weakened. Here, we can say it really was for other debts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing a real difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the oxen case the borrower tied the payment to one specific deal, and the lender admits that deal happened. So the claim of another loan has nothing to stand on, and the שטר is weakened. In the plain case the borrower only said 'I paid you,' so the payment could easily have been for other debts, and the שטר stays strong.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב פפא, a general claim of 'I paid you' does not weaken a שטר if the lender says the payment was for other debts. When the payment is tied to one specific deal that the lender admits, the שטר is weakened.

phrases.english: There, since he said:
You gave it to me for oxen and you took it from oxen
the document is weakened;
here, say that they were other [debts].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 7
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both cases are the same: the lender admits payment and claims it was for other debts.
steps.terutzMaskana: A payment tied to a specific admitted deal weakens the שטר. A general payment can be assumed to be for other debts.

steps.title: What is the final ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the bottom line on the dispute about the weakened שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: What was decided about this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the final outcome is in the debate from step 6. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 6–8 showed two views on whether the שטר is weakened, and they defended רב פפא's position. Now the גמרא wants the practical conclusion.

keyTerms.meaning: What came of it? (What is the final ruling?)

phrases.english: What was concluded about it?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the case from step 5: the borrower says he paid, and the lender says it was for other loans.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רב פפא's view in step 8, the גמרא asks for the final ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical הלכה: is the שטר weakened or not?

steps.title: Two later אמוראים disagree
steps.stepSummary: רב פפי says the שטר is not weakened. רב ששת בריה דרב אידי says it is weakened.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפי said: the שטר is not weakened. רב ששת son of רב אידי said: the שטר is weakened.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports that the question was still debated by two later אמוראים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפי holds that the lender's claim of 'other debts' is reasonable, so the שטר keeps its full strength. רב ששת בריה דרב אידי holds that the payment casts doubt on the שטר, so it is weakened.

keyTerms.meaning: The document is weakened (its power to collect is damaged)

steps.confusionAlert: רב פפי here is not the same person as רב פפא from steps 6–8. The names look alike, but they are two different אמוראים.

phrases.aramaic: רַב פַּפֵּי אָמַר: לָא אִיתְּרַע שְׁטָרָא.
phrases.english: Rav Pappi said: the document is not weakened.

phrases.aramaic: רַב שֵׁשֶׁת בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi said:
the document is weakened.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פַּפֵּי אָמַר: לָא אִיתְּרַע שְׁטָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by showing that the dispute continued among later Amoraim.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The question remained in dispute: רב פפי says the שטר is not weakened, and רב ששת בריה דרב אידי says it is.

steps.title: The ruling: the document is weakened
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה follows the view that the שטר is weakened.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: the שטר is weakened.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final practical ruling: the שטר is weakened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender cannot simply collect with the שטר by saying the earlier payment was for other debts. His document has lost some of its strength.
steps.whatToRemember: When the borrower paid and the lender claims it was for other loans, the הלכה is that the שטר is weakened.

phrases.english: And the law is: the document is weakened.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute from step 10.

steps.title: The ruling applies only to payment in front of witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The שטר is weakened only when the payment was made before witnesses. A private payment does not weaken it, because the lender has a מיגו.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies when he paid in front of witnesses and did not mention the שטר. But if he paid privately, just between the two of them, the lender could have said 'it never happened.' So he is also believed when he says 'it was for other debts.' This is like the case of אבימי son of רבי אבהו.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the ruling from step 11. It only applies when witnesses saw the payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With witnesses, the lender cannot deny receiving money, so his 'other debts' claim weakens the שטר. With no witnesses, he could have denied getting anything at all. Since he chose the smaller claim, we believe him because of a מיגו.

keyTerms.meaning: Since he could have made a stronger claim, we believe his weaker one

steps.whatToRemember: The שטר is weakened only when the payment was witnessed. In a private payment, the lender's מיגו protects his claim of 'other debts.'

phrases.english: And this applies when he paid him in front of witnesses
and did not mention the document to him;
but if he paid him just between the two of them,
since the lender could say
"it never happened,"
he can also say "it was for other debts,"
and this is like the case of Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu.
phrases.notes: This points to a known story (כתובות 85a) where אבימי paid without witnesses and the lender claimed it was for another debt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling from step 11 to a witnessed payment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A private payment does not weaken the שטר, because the lender has a מיגו that he could have denied receiving anything.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that witnesses to the payment are exactly what weakens the שטר. Without them, the lender's power to deny everything makes him believable.

steps.title: 'I'll believe you' and then paying before witnesses
steps.stepSummary: A borrower told the lender he would believe him whenever he said he wasn't paid. Then he paid in front of witnesses. אביי and רבא say the lender is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man said to his friend: 'You are believed by me whenever you tell me I did not pay.' He went and paid him in front of witnesses. אביי and רבא both said: he made him believable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new case about a borrower who made the lender trustworthy. אביי and רבא rule that the lender can still collect, even though witnesses saw the payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower agreed in advance to accept the lender's word about non-payment. אביי and רבא hold that this promise holds even against witnesses who saw him pay.

keyTerms.meaning: You are believed by me (I trust your word)

phrases.english: A certain man said to his fellow:
phrases.notes: The borrower is the one talking here, to the man who lent him money.

phrases.english: "You are believed by me whenever
you tell me 'I did not pay.'"
He went and paid him in front of witnesses.
Abaye and Rava both said:
But he made him believable.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: מְהֵימְנַתְּ לִי כֹּל אֵימַת דְּאָמְרַתְּ לִי לָא פָּרַעְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the weakened-שטר topic to a related topic: a borrower's promise to believe the lender.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to אביי and רבא, the lender is believed against witnesses because the borrower made him believable.

steps.title: רב פפא: the promise doesn't beat witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא objects. The borrower trusted the lender more than himself, but not more than witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא objected: Granted, he trusted him more than himself. But did he trust him more than witnesses?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא challenges אביי and רבא's ruling from step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The promise meant: 'If it's my word against yours, I'll accept yours.' It never meant the lender would beat actual witnesses. So the payment before witnesses counts, and the borrower is free.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa objected to this:
Granted that he trusted him more than himself,
did he trust him more than witnesses?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly attacks the ruling of אביי and רבא in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי and רבא's ruling that the lender is believed against witnesses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The borrower's promise only gave the lender priority over the borrower's own word, not over witnesses.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a promise of trust is read narrowly. It only covers what the person actually meant to give up.

steps.title: Trusted 'like two', but paid before three
steps.stepSummary: A borrower trusted the lender 'like two witnesses' and then paid before three. רב פפא rules that the promise does not cover three.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man said to his friend: 'You are believed by me like two witnesses whenever you say I did not pay.' He went and paid him in front of three. רב פפא said: he trusted him like two; he did not trust him like three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related case and רב פפא's ruling on it. Three witnesses outweigh a lender who was only trusted like two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower set an exact level of trust: equal to two witnesses. Since he paid in front of three, the payment is proven beyond the trust he gave. This matches רב פפא's reasoning in step 14: a promise only covers what it says.
steps.whatToRemember: A promise to trust the lender is limited to its exact terms. 'More than me' is not 'more than witnesses,' and 'like two' is not 'like three.'

phrases.english: A certain man said to his fellow:
"You are believed by me like two witnesses,
whenever you say 'I did not pay.'"
He went and paid him in front of three.
Rav Pappa said:
He trusted him like two;
he did not trust him like three.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: מְהֵימְנַתְּ לִי כְּבֵי תְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up case using the same idea from step 14: a trust promise is limited to its stated terms.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trust 'like two witnesses' does not override three witnesses, so the borrower is free.

steps.title: Majority counts for estimates, not for testimony
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע argues that 'following the majority' applies only to estimating value. In testimony, two witnesses equal a hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב יהושע said to רב פפא: Fine, the חכמים say we follow the majority of opinions. But that is only for estimating value, because more people means more expertise. For testimony, a hundred witnesses are like two, and two are like a hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא challenges רב פפא's ruling that three witnesses beat the lender's 'like two witnesses' trust.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא treated three as stronger than two. רב הונא says numbers only matter when people give opinions, like estimating a price. In testimony, two kosher witnesses already give full proof, so three add nothing, and the lender stays believed.

keyTerms.meaning: an estimate or assessment, such as of value

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think more witnesses always make a stronger case. In עדות, two kosher witnesses are already complete proof.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key rule: counting heads matters for opinions and estimates, but not for testimony.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְרַב פָּפָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said to Rav Pappa:
Granted that the Sages said
that we follow the majority of opinions,
that applies to estimating value,
because the more people there are, the more expert they are;
but regarding testimony,
a hundred are like two, and two are like a hundred!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְרַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's ruling in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that 'like two' does not cover three witnesses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Majority rule applies only to estimates. In testimony, two and three witnesses are exactly equal, so three cannot outweigh 'like two'.

steps.title: Second version of the case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא retells the case in another version. Someone trusted the lender 'like two witnesses' and then paid before three, and רב פפא gives the same ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: A man told his fellow, 'You are believed by me like two witnesses whenever you say I didn't pay.' He went and paid him in front of three. רב פפא said: He trusted him like two, not like three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the story. This sets up a different form of רב הונא's response.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The facts and רב פפא's ruling are the same as before. What changes in this version is how רב הונא answers, which comes in the next steps.
steps.confusionAlert: The story and רב פפא's words match the first version. The difference between the versions is only in רב הונא's reply.

phrases.english: Another version:
There was a man who said to his fellow:
"You are believed by me like two witnesses
whenever you say: I did not repay."
phrases.notes: He means: whenever you say that I, the borrower, did not pay you.

phrases.english: He went and repaid him in front of three.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כְּבֵי תְרֵי הֵימְנֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: He trusted him like two,
he did not trust him like three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second telling of the case from step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trust 'like two' does not stand against three witnesses.

steps.title: Two witnesses equal a hundred
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, רב הונא again objects that two witnesses are the same as a hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב יהושע objected: Two are like a hundred, and a hundred are like two!
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא challenges רב פפא again. Three witnesses are no stronger than two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the borrower said 'like two,' and two witnesses are full testimony, the promise already covers any number of witnesses. So paying before three changes nothing.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objected to it:
Two are like a hundred, and a hundred are like two!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to רב פפא's ruling in the second version.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling in the second version
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In testimony, number does not matter, so 'like two' already covers three.

steps.title: Saying 'like three' turns it into counting opinions
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא agrees that if the borrower said 'like three' and paid before four, the four win. By naming more than two, he moved into the world of opinions.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he had said 'like three,' and then paid him in front of four, then since he moved into opinions, he moved into opinions.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא adds a case where he agrees the bigger number wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two witnesses are already full testimony, so saying 'like three' only makes sense if he is counting people the way we count opinions. Once he counts that way, four beat three, and the lender is not believed.
steps.whatToRemember: Saying 'like two' is about testimony, where two equal a hundred. Saying 'like three' or more turns it into counting opinions, so a larger group wins.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the exact words of a promise decide which rule applies: the rule of testimony or the rule of majority.

phrases.english: But if he said to him "like three,"
and went and repaid him in front of four,
since he moved into opinions, he has moved into opinions.
phrases.notes: Two witnesses already make full testimony, so naming three means he was counting people like opinions, and then four beat three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב הונא's words, adding a case where the number does count.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the promise names a number above two, it becomes a count of opinions, and a larger group of witnesses beats it.

steps.title: Why no oath on a minor's claim?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: no oath is taken on the claim of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, and a קטן is not made to swear. It then asks why.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not swear about the claim of a חרש, a שוטה, or a קטן, and we do not make a קטן swear. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה and asks for its source. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that a claim from someone without legal understanding does not create an oath. The גמרא wants to know where this comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: a deaf-mute, who is not legally responsible
a person who is mentally not competent

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל טַעֲנַת חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן,
phrases.english: We do not swear about the claim of a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor,
and we do not make a minor swear.
What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for why a minor's claim does not create an oath.

steps.title: A minor's handing over means nothing
steps.stepSummary: The answer comes from the פסוק 'כי יתן איש': the oath is said about a grown man handing over property. What a minor hands over has no legal weight.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'If a man gives his fellow money or vessels to guard.' And a minor's giving is nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק from the section about oaths over deposits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath in that section begins with a person handing over property. The פסוק says 'איש,' a man, and a minor's handing over has no legal force. So his claim cannot lead to an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: is nothing, has no legal weight

steps.whatToRemember: No oath on a minor's claim: the oath is said about 'איש' handing over property, and a minor's handing over means nothing legally.

phrases.english: The verse says:
"If a man gives to his fellow
money or vessels to guard,"
and a minor's giving is nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק speaks about a man handing over property, and a minor's handing over has no legal weight, so his claim cannot lead to an oath.

steps.title: The משנה seems to contradict itself about a minor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line that we do take an oath to a קטן and to הקדש. It then asks how that fits with the earlier line saying no oath is taken on a קטן's claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'But we do swear to a קטן and to הקדש.' But didn't you say in the first part that we do not swear on the claim of a שוטה or a קטן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and shows that it seems to clash with the line we just learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 21 we learned that a minor's claim carries no legal weight, so no oath is taken because of it. Now the same משנה says we DO swear 'to a קטן.' Both lines can't seem to be true together.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of the משנה
'But didn't you say?' A phrase that points out a contradiction

phrases.english: But one does swear to a minor and to Temple property.
But didn't you say in the first part:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל טַעֲנַת שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן!
phrases.english: One does not swear on the claim of an imbecile or a minor!
phrases.notes: This is the line we just learned in step 20.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the משנה's second line against its first line, which was explained in steps 20-21.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first part of the משנה says a קטן's claim brings no oath, so how can the second part say an oath is taken to a קטן?

steps.title: רב: it is about someone claiming his father's debt
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that the 'קטן' in the second line is a person who comes claiming a debt owed to his late father. This ruling follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: It is talking about one who comes with his father's claim, and it follows the view of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: רב resolves the contradiction by saying the second line is about a different kind of case. He also names the תנא it follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first line is about a real child, whose claim means nothing. The second line is about someone claiming money owed to his father, who doesn't really know the details. רב says that even so an oath is taken, and this follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

keyTerms.meaning: Coming to court with his father's claim

phrases.english: Rav said: It is about one who comes with his father's claim,
and it follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The two lines are about different cases, and the second line follows one specific תנא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both lines talk about the same real child.
steps.terutzMaskana: The second line is about an heir claiming his father's debt, following רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

steps.title: The ברייתא of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב makes a man swear when he admits to the son that he owed the father a מנה and says he paid back half. The חכמים say this man is like someone returning a lost item and is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: Sometimes a person swears because of his own claim. How so? He says to someone, 'Your father had a מנה with me, and I paid him back half.' He must swear, and that is the case of swearing on his own claim. The חכמים say: He is only like someone returning a lost item, and he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא that is the source for רב's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son did not know about the debt, and the man told him about it on his own. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב still makes him swear about the half he says he paid. The חכמים say that someone who volunteers information like this is like a person returning a lost object, so he does not have to swear.

keyTerms.meaning: His own claim, meaning the oath comes from what he himself said
A sum of one hundred זוז
One who returns a lost item

steps.confusionAlert: 'His own claim' does not mean he is claiming money. It means nobody demanded anything from him, and only his own words brought the oath.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:

phrases.aramaic: פְּעָמִים שֶׁאָדָם נִשְׁבָּע עַל טַעֲנַת עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: There are times a person swears because of his own claim.
How so? He said to him:
'Your father had a maneh in my hands,
and I paid him back half' –
this man swears,
and this is the one who swears because of his own claim.
And the Sages say:
He is only like one returning a lost item, and is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for רב's statement that the line follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.raayaObject: That according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב an oath is taken in a case of a father's debt that the son doesn't know about.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא with the case of 'מנה לאביך בידי'

steps.title: Doesn't he agree a returner of lost items is exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבי אליעזר בן יעקב really rejects the well-known rule that someone returning a lost item does not have to swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does רבי אליעזר בן יעקב not hold that one who returns a lost item is exempt?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's ruling in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that someone returning a lost item is exempt from an oath is accepted by everyone. If the man volunteered the debt himself, he looks exactly like a returner of a lost item. So why would רבי אליעזר בן יעקב make him swear?

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov –
doesn't he hold that one who returns a lost item is exempt?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the view of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב in the ברייתא brought in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's ruling that the man swears
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The man volunteered the debt himself, like someone returning a lost item, and such a person is exempt from an oath.

steps.title: רב: the son did make a claim
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that in the ברייתא the son claimed the debt from the man, so the man was not volunteering anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: It is a case where a קטן made a claim against him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the challenge by adding a detail to the case: the son had claimed the debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the son demanded the money, the man's admission of half was an answer to a claim. That makes it a normal case of admitting part of a claim, and not a case of returning a lost item. That is why he swears.

keyTerms.meaning: He made a claim against him

phrases.english: Rav said: When a minor made a claim against him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a detail to the case: there was a claim, so he is not volunteering like a returner of a lost item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The man brought up the debt on his own.
steps.terutzMaskana: The son claimed the debt, so the man was answering a claim.

steps.title: But a minor's claim doesn't count
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a קטן's claim cannot bring an oath, since the משנה says we do not swear on the claim of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A minor?! But you said we do not swear on the claim of a חרש, a שוטה, or a קטן!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's answer, using the first line of our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said the son's claim makes this a real claim. But a minor's claim has no legal weight (step 21). So how can it lead to an oath?

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is not mentally competent

phrases.english: A minor?!
But you said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל טַעֲנַת חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן!
phrases.english: One does not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's answer in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's statement that a קטן made the claim
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says a minor's claim brings no oath.

steps.title: He is really an adult, called 'minor' about his father's matters
steps.stepSummary: The son is really an adult. He is called a 'קטן' only because he knows as little about his father's business as a child would.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, he is an adult. So why is he called a minor? Because when it comes to his father's matters, he is like a minor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'קטן' here is not about age. It describes how little the son knows about his father's dealings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An adult son's claim does count legally, so it can bring an oath. He is called 'קטן' because, like a child, he doesn't know the details of his father's loans. This also explains our משנה's line 'נשבעין לקטן': it means an adult heir claiming his father's debt.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Really' or 'actually,' used to keep a case while explaining it differently

steps.whatToRemember: The 'קטן' in 'נשבעין לקטן' is an adult heir claiming his father's debt. He is called a 'minor' only because he doesn't know the details. The ruling that an oath is taken follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'קטן' here as a child. It means an adult who knows as little as a child about his father's business.

phrases.english: Really, he is an adult,
and why do they call him a minor?
Because regarding his father's matters – he is a minor.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם גָּדוֹל, וְאַמַּאי קָרוּ לֵיהּ קָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 27 and settles the contradiction from step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the word 'קטן' to mean someone who doesn't know the facts, not someone young in age.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The claimant is a real minor, whose claim has no legal weight.
steps.terutzMaskana: The claimant is an adult heir, called 'קטן' because he doesn't know about his father's dealings.
steps.whyThisMatters: It settles both the ברייתא and the משנה's line 'נשבעין לקטן' as being about an adult heir.

steps.title: Why call it 'his own claim' if the son made the claim?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא: if the son is the one who claimed, the oath should not be called 'his own claim.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does the ברייתא say 'his own claim'? It is a claim made by others!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the answer that the son made the claim. Now it points out that the words of the ברייתא do not seem to fit that answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 said the oath comes because the son claimed the money. But the ברייתא describes this oath as coming from 'his own claim' (טענת עצמו). If the son started the claim, it looks like a claim of others (טענת אחרים), not the man's own.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if what you just said is true
A claim made by other people

phrases.english: If so, why 'his own claim'?!
phrases.notes: The quoted words come from the ברייתא in step 24, which calls this oath one that comes from 'his own claim.'

phrases.english: It is a claim of others!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the answer that the son is an adult who made the claim, then attacks the ברייתא's wording based on that answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'טענת עצמו' as read under רב's explanation that the son made the claim.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the son made the claim, the oath comes from someone else's claim, so calling it 'his own claim' seems to be the wrong wording.

steps.title: The claim is from others, but the admission is his own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the claim came from the son, but the man's partial admission came from himself, and that is why the ברייתא says 'his own.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a claim of others, together with his own admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the wording. The son made the claim, but the man himself admitted to part of it, and that admission is the 'his own' part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath like this needs two pieces: someone claims, and the man admits to part of the claim. Here the claim came from the son, but the admission ('I paid back half, so I owe the other half') came from the man's own mouth. The ברייתא's phrase 'his own' points to that admission.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who admits to part of a claim and must swear about the rest

steps.whatToRemember: The son, an adult who knows little about his father's business, makes the claim. The man admits to part of it on his own. Claim from others plus his own admission means he must swear, according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

phrases.english: A claim of others, and his own admission.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge of step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the wording: 'his own' refers to the admission, not the claim.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'His own claim' seemed to mean that the man himself started the claim, which would clash with the son being the claimant.
steps.terutzMaskana: The claim comes from others (the son), while the admission comes from the man himself, so the wording fits.
